moments.title: The Triple Alliance is signed
moments.body: Otto von Bismarck, German Chancellor, builds a defensive alliance to isolate France after the Franco-Prussian War (1870-71). The treaty is secret. Europe's diplomatic order over the next 32 years calcifies around two blocs.

quote.text: The great questions of the day will not be settled by speeches and majority decisions... but by iron and blood.
quote.attrib: Bismarck, speech to the Prussian Landtag, 1862

moments.takeaway: WWI's alliance structure was built decades before the war and was designed for the previous century's balance of power.

moments.title: The Triple Entente takes shape
moments.body: France and Russia had allied in 1894. The Entente Cordiale (1904) settled colonial disputes between Britain and France. The Anglo-Russian Convention (1907) does the same with Russia. None is a binding military alliance — but they create an expectation of mutual support that will pull all three into 1914.
moments.takeaway: Britain enters WWI without a formal treaty commitment to France. The Belgian neutrality treaty of 1839 provides the legal pretext.

moments.title: The July Crisis
moments.who: All the great powers, in five weeks
moments.body: 28 June: Archduke Franz Ferdinand is assassinated in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip. 23 July: Austria-Hungary issues an ultimatum to Serbia designed to be rejected. 28 July: Austria declares war on Serbia. 1 August: Germany declares war on Russia. 3 August: Germany declares war on France. 4 August: Britain declares war on Germany after the invasion of Belgium.

quote.text: The lamps are going out all over Europe, we shall not see them lit again in our life-time.
quote.attrib: Edward Grey, British Foreign Secretary, 3 August 1914

moments.takeaway: Once mobilisation began (especially Russia's), railway timetables and military logic made standing down almost impossible. AJP Taylor's 'War by Timetable' argument.

now.title: Why WWI still matters
now.body: The borders of the modern Middle East (Sykes-Picot, 1916), the collapse of four empires (German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian, Ottoman), the Treaty of Versailles's role in setting up WWII, the redrawing of Europe — all flow from the war. The 'Christmas truce' image of pity meets the industrial slaughter of the Somme and Verdun.
now.open_questions: Was WWI inevitable? Christopher Clark's 'The Sleepwalkers' (2012) argues no — it was a contingent failure of statesmen. Max Hastings's 'Catastrophe' argues Germany bears more responsibility than Clark allows. The debate is alive.

items.reflection: 1914 is the case study in how systems designed for stability can produce catastrophe. The alliance structure, the army timetables, the press, the personalities — none individually wanted total war. They got it anyway.

moments.title: The February Revolution
moments.who: Petrograd workers, soldiers and the Duma
moments.body: Russia is collapsing under WWI. Bread shortages in Petrograd trigger strikes; soldiers refuse to fire on protesters; Tsar Nicholas II abdicates on 15 March (2 March OS). A Provisional Government under Prince Lvov (later Kerensky) shares power awkwardly with the Petrograd Soviet of Workers' and Soldiers' Deputies.
moments.takeaway: The Tsar fell before Lenin returned from exile. The Bolsheviks did not make the February Revolution.

moments.title: Lenin returns in a sealed train
moments.body: The German government provides a sealed train through Germany to Sweden, calculating that Lenin will destabilise Russia and take it out of the war. Lenin arrives at the Finland Station, Petrograd, on 16 April and issues the April Theses — 'all power to the Soviets', no support for the Provisional Government, immediate peace.

quote.text: Peace, land, and bread.
quote.attrib: Bolshevik slogan, 1917

moments.takeaway: German intelligence calculated correctly. By November the Bolsheviks had seized power and signed a separate peace (Brest-Litovsk, March 1918).

moments.title: The October Revolution
moments.who: The Bolsheviks under Lenin and Trotsky
moments.body: On 7 November (25 October OS), Bolshevik forces seize the Winter Palace in Petrograd. Trotsky organises the Military Revolutionary Committee. Kerensky flees. The Bolsheviks issue the Decree on Peace and the Decree on Land within hours.
moments.takeaway: The 'storming' of the Winter Palace was largely a Soviet propaganda image (especially Eisenstein's 1928 film). The actual takeover was smaller and less dramatic — but no less consequential.

now.title: The shadow of 1917
now.body: The Soviet Union lasted 74 years. The Cold War, Mao's revolution in China (1949), Castro's in Cuba (1959), Vietnam, the entire 20th-century communist project — all trace back to that November in Petrograd. The collapse of 1991 closed one cycle; Putin's reading of Russian history (his 'greatest geopolitical catastrophe' line) opens another.
now.open_questions: Was October 1917 a coup or a revolution? Soviet historiography insisted on revolution. Western Cold War scholarship often called it a coup. Sheila Fitzpatrick and Stephen Kotkin have argued for more nuanced 'revolution from above with popular elements' framings.

items.reflection: Revolutions don't happen because of one cause. War, famine, a discredited monarchy, a weak provisional government, a disciplined party with a plausible programme — Russia in 1917 had all of them.

moments.title: The Nuremberg Laws
moments.body: The Reich Citizenship Law and the Law for the Protection of German Blood and German Honour strip Jews of German citizenship and ban marriage between Jews and 'Aryans'. They legally codify what propaganda had been preparing.
moments.takeaway: The Holocaust was not unleashed at one moment. It was built in stages, each one normalising the next.

moments.title: Kristallnacht
moments.who: SA and SS units, with civilian participation
moments.body: On 9-10 November, Nazi forces destroy 267 synagogues, smash 7,500 Jewish-owned businesses, and arrest around 30,000 Jewish men, sending them to concentration camps. The pretext was the assassination of a German diplomat in Paris by a Jewish teenager, Herschel Grynszpan.

quote.text: I should not wish to be a Jew in Germany.
quote.attrib: Hermann Göring, immediately after Kristallnacht

moments.takeaway: Western governments protested but offered few visas. The Évian Conference (July 1938) had already failed to coordinate refugee admission.

moments.title: The Wannsee Conference
moments.who: Reinhard Heydrich and 14 senior Nazi officials
moments.body: At a villa in the Berlin suburb of Wannsee, Heydrich convenes a 90-minute meeting to coordinate the 'Final Solution' across German ministries. By this point mass killings are already underway — the Einsatzgruppen have shot perhaps 500,000 Jews in the East, and Chelmno extermination camp is operating. Wannsee codifies industrial-scale murder.
moments.takeaway: Wannsee did not initiate the Holocaust. It bureaucratised it. The minutes (the Wannsee Protocol) were preserved by chance — copy 16 of 30 survived.

now.title: Memory and denial
now.body: Six million Jews were murdered, alongside Roma, disabled people, Soviet POWs, gay men, political opponents and others. Yad Vashem, the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum and the Imperial War Museum in London preserve testimony. Holocaust denial is a criminal offence in Germany, Austria, France and elsewhere. Eyewitness survivors are now mostly in their 90s; the transition to history-without-witnesses is happening now.
now.open_questions: The historians' debate (Historikerstreit) of the 1980s asked whether the Holocaust was unique or comparable to other 20th-century atrocities. Saul Friedländer's two-volume history argues for both specificity (the elimination of European Jewry as ideological project) and connection to wider patterns of mass violence.

items.reflection: The Holocaust forces every other historical question to be asked more carefully. How does a modern industrial state mobilise for genocide? Who participates? Who looks away? Who resists?

moments.title: Churchill's Fulton speech
moments.who: Winston Churchill, at Westminster College, Missouri
moments.body: Out of office, Churchill warns of an 'iron curtain' descending across Europe. Stalin responds furiously. The phrase, though not new (it had been used by Goebbels and others), becomes the defining image of postwar Europe.

quote.text: From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent.
quote.attrib: Churchill, 5 March 1946

moments.takeaway: Public framing matters. Churchill's speech named the conflict before policymakers had agreed there was one.

moments.title: Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan
moments.body: March 1947: Truman pledges aid to Greece and Turkey to resist communist insurgency. June 1947: Marshall announces a European Recovery Programme. $13 billion (around $150 billion in 2020 dollars) flows to Western Europe over four years. Containment, as defined by George Kennan's 1946 'Long Telegram' and 1947 X-Article, becomes US policy.
moments.takeaway: The Cold War was framed economically as much as militarily. Marshall Aid bought a generation of Western European stability.

moments.title: Cuban Missile Crisis
moments.body: Soviet missiles in Cuba are detected by US U-2 reconnaissance on 14 October. For 13 days the world stands at the edge of nuclear war. Kennedy imposes a 'quarantine' (blockade would be an act of war). Khrushchev removes the missiles in exchange for a US pledge not to invade Cuba and the secret removal of Jupiter missiles from Turkey.
moments.takeaway: The hotline (Moscow-Washington direct line) was installed after the crisis. Both leaders had been closer to losing control than the public knew.

now.title: After 1991
now.body: The Soviet Union dissolved on 26 December 1991. NATO expanded east through the 1990s and 2000s. The 'end of history' (Fukuyama, 1989) was contested almost immediately by Samuel Huntington's clash-of-civilisations frame. Russia's wars in Georgia (2008), Ukraine (2014, 2022) have been read by many historians as a return of great-power rivalry — though the alignments differ.
now.open_questions: Was the Cold War 'won' by the West, or did the USSR collapse under internal contradictions? John Lewis Gaddis argues for Reagan-era pressure; Stephen Kotkin emphasises internal Soviet dynamics. Both are right in part.

items.reflection: The Cold War shaped almost everything from 1945 to 1991: decolonisation, the welfare state, civil rights, popular culture, science. To understand the late 20th century, you have to see it through that prism.

moments.title: Edward the Confessor dies
moments.body: Edward dies on 5 January 1066 without a clear heir. The Witan elects Harold Godwinson, Earl of Wessex. William of Normandy claims Edward had promised him the throne; Harald Hardrada of Norway claims it through the older Cnut succession. Three claimants — one crown.
moments.takeaway: 1066 is the year of three kings of England: Edward, Harold and William.

moments.title: Stamford Bridge and Hastings
moments.body: 25 September: Harold defeats Hardrada and Tostig at Stamford Bridge near York. 28 September: William lands at Pevensey. 14 October: Harold marches south and is killed at the Battle of Hastings. William is crowned at Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066.

quote.text: Then King Edward came to Westminster towards midwinter, and there had consecrated that minster which he himself had built.
quote.attrib: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, 1065-66

moments.takeaway: Two battles in three weeks decided the succession. The exhaustion of Stamford Bridge shaped the outcome at Hastings.

moments.title: Domesday Book completed
moments.body: Commissioned at Gloucester at Christmas 1085, the survey records over 13,000 places, every plough, mill, fishpond and noble landholder. It is the most detailed administrative document in medieval Europe.
moments.takeaway: The Conquest created a centralised, taxed, surveyed state in a way Anglo-Saxon England had only partly been.

now.title: 1066 in the modern imagination
now.body: The Bayeux Tapestry (probably 1070s-80s, embroidered in Canterbury) remains in Normandy. 'In 1066' is still shorthand for a deep cultural break — Norman French in law and administration, English as the speech of the common people. The Tower of London, Westminster Hall and a Norman elite stamped on parish churches across the country.
now.open_questions: Was the Conquest a brutal replacement of an elite, or a gradual layering? David Bates and others have shown the Anglo-Saxon administrative system was largely preserved — it was the landholders, not the institutions, that were replaced.

items.reflection: 1066 is the date every schoolchild knows. Its significance is real — a conquest, a new language layer, a new aristocracy — but its meaning was made by what was kept (the shires, the writs) as much as what was destroyed.

moments.title: Runnymede
moments.body: After military failures in France (loss of Normandy 1204) and heavy taxation, the barons rebelled. At Runnymede on 15 June 1215, John attached his seal to the Articles of the Barons. The fuller Charter of Liberties (Magna Carta) followed within days.

quote.text: No free man shall be seized or imprisoned... except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land.
quote.attrib: Magna Carta, clause 39 (1215)

moments.takeaway: Clauses 39 and 40 are the source of due process traditions. Most of the original 63 clauses are about specific feudal grievances — fish-weirs, forest law, scutage.

moments.title: Annulled by the Pope
moments.body: On 24 August 1215, Pope Innocent III's bull declares Magna Carta 'null and void of all validity forever'. Civil war resumes; the barons invite Prince Louis of France to take the throne.
moments.takeaway: Magna Carta failed in 1215 as a peace treaty. Its reissues (1216, 1217, 1225, 1297) under Henry III and Edward I are what survived.

now.title: Foundational myth and real law
now.body: Three clauses of the 1297 reissue remain on English statute books today, including clause 29 (descended from clause 39). Magna Carta as 'foundation of liberty' is largely the construction of Sir Edward Coke in the 17th century, used against the Stuarts. The US founders cited it constantly. Four original 1215 copies survive — two at the British Library, one each at Lincoln and Salisbury cathedrals.
now.open_questions: How much of Magna Carta is rhetoric versus law? Sir James Holt's 'Magna Carta' (1965, 1992) treats it both as a baronial treaty of its moment and as a document whose later use was not accidental — the framers genuinely tried to bind the crown.

items.reflection: A failed 13th-century peace treaty became, by deliberate later use, the symbolic charter of constitutional government. Both the original failure and the later reinvention are part of its meaning.

moments.title: Plague reaches Crimea and Constantinople
moments.body: Yersinia pestis reaches the Genoese port of Caffa during a Mongol siege. Gabriele de' Mussi later wrote (probably with embellishment) that besiegers catapulted plague corpses into the city. Genoese ships carry the disease to Sicily in October 1347.
moments.takeaway: The plague moved along trade routes. Globalisation existed in 1347 — and its diseases moved at the speed of merchant ships.

moments.title: England and northern Europe
moments.body: Plague reaches Melcombe Regis (Weymouth) around June 1348. London by autumn. Mortality probably 40-60% across England. Whole villages depopulated; church records, manorial rolls and parish lists record the impact.

quote.text: There died at Avignon in three days 1,800 persons.
quote.attrib: Gabriele de' Mussi, Historia de Morbo, c. 1348

moments.takeaway: The plague returned in waves through 1361, 1369, 1375 and beyond — a permanent demographic shadow.

moments.title: Statute of Labourers
moments.body: Labour shortages drove up wages. Parliament tried to peg wages at pre-plague rates. The Statute was widely flouted. Real wages roughly doubled across the late 14th century. Serfdom weakened as labour mobility increased.
moments.takeaway: Economic consequences of mortality reshaped class relations. The 1381 Peasants' Revolt was one downstream consequence.

now.title: Disease as historical force
now.body: Modern genomics (Spyrou et al., 2022) traced Black Death origins to the Tian Shan region around 1338. The plague reshaped European economy, religion, art (the Dance of Death), and the social position of survivors. COVID-19 (2020-2023) revived comparative interest. Plague is still present in the world; the WHO records around 1,000-2,000 cases a year, mostly in Madagascar, the DRC and Peru.
now.open_questions: Was the Black Death decisive for the late medieval shift from feudalism, or just an accelerant? Robert Brenner's debate with M. M. Postan argued exactly this question.

items.reflection: Mortality at this scale resets societies. Wages, religion, art, gender norms, urban-rural balance — all shifted. The plague is one of the strongest cases for treating disease as a historical actor in its own right.

moments.title: First Battle of St Albans
moments.body: 22 May 1455: Richard, Duke of York, defeats Henry VI's forces at St Albans. The Duke of Somerset is killed. Henry VI — periodically incapacitated by mental illness — is captured. The first action of what becomes a 32-year dynastic war.
moments.takeaway: The roots lie earlier: Henry VI's weakness, factional politics, the loss of France in 1453 destabilising the regime.

moments.title: Towton
moments.body: 29 March 1461 (Palm Sunday): Edward IV defeats Lancastrian forces at Towton in Yorkshire. Possibly the bloodiest battle on English soil — contemporary accounts put deaths at 28,000, modern estimates lower but still in the tens of thousands.
moments.takeaway: Edward IV's reign (1461-83) was relatively stable. The wars renewed under his son Edward V and brother Richard III.

moments.title: Bosworth Field
moments.body: 22 August 1485: Henry Tudor defeats Richard III, who is killed in the fighting — the last English king to die in battle. Henry becomes Henry VII. He marries Elizabeth of York in 1486, founding the Tudor dynasty.

quote.text: Treason! Treason! Treason!
quote.attrib: Richard III, allegedly at Bosworth, in the Croyland Chronicle account

moments.takeaway: Richard's remains were lost until rediscovered under a Leicester car park in 2012, identified by DNA and scoliosis evidence.

now.title: Tudor mythmaking
now.body: Polydore Vergil and Thomas More wrote Tudor-era histories blackening Richard III. Shakespeare's 'Richard III' (c. 1593) cemented the image. Modern revisionism (the Richard III Society, founded 1924) has rebalanced — Richard's administrative record was competent; the Princes in the Tower remain genuinely unresolved.
now.open_questions: Did Richard kill the Princes? The case is circumstantial. Henry VII had motive too. Alison Weir, Philippa Langley and David Horspool have argued opposing positions on the same evidence.

items.reflection: Dynastic war is messy: shifting allegiances, no clean ideological line, generations of revenge. The Tudor narrative of unity restored after chaos is itself a piece of political work.

moments.title: Henry's 'Great Matter' begins
moments.who: Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon
moments.body: Henry, having no male heir from Catherine, seeks annulment. Pope Clement VII — a prisoner of Catherine's nephew Charles V after the 1527 Sack of Rome — refuses. Cardinal Wolsey fails to deliver and falls in 1529.
moments.takeaway: The English Reformation begins as a dynastic crisis with a geopolitical lock — the Pope cannot defy the Emperor.

moments.title: The Break with Rome
moments.body: January 1533: Henry secretly marries Anne Boleyn. May 1533: Cranmer annuls the Catherine marriage. 1534: Act of Supremacy declares Henry 'Supreme Head' of the Church of England. Thomas More refuses the Oath of Succession and is executed in 1535.

quote.text: The King's good servant, but God's first.
quote.attrib: Thomas More, scaffold speech, 6 July 1535

moments.takeaway: The Reformation in England is enacted by Parliament under royal direction — a top-down political settlement rather than a popular religious revival.

moments.title: Dissolution of the Monasteries
moments.who: Thomas Cromwell and the Court of Augmentations
moments.body: Smaller houses dissolved 1536; larger ones 1538-41. Around 800 religious houses closed; over 10,000 monks, nuns and friars displaced. The Pilgrimage of Grace (October 1536) — perhaps 40,000 northern rebels — was suppressed by Henry's broken promises.
moments.takeaway: Crown wealth doubled briefly; most land was sold to gentry buyers, creating a class invested in not reversing the Reformation.

now.title: Five centuries of consequence
now.body: The Church of England remains established. The Royal Supremacy survives in form — the monarch is still Supreme Governor. Catholic emancipation came only in 1829. Eamon Duffy, Diarmaid MacCulloch and Alec Ryrie have produced the modern scholarly synthesis: a slow, contested, top-down change with deep popular reluctance.
now.open_questions: Was the English Reformation Henry VIII's personal project that became something else, or a wider movement Henry rode? The balance has shifted with each generation of historians.

items.reflection: Personal motives (a male heir, Anne Boleyn, monastic wealth) and structural pressures (Lutheran Reformation, fiscal need, Pope's captivity) collide in 1533-34. Both readings — accident and inevitability — capture part of the truth.

moments.title: Elizabeth's accession
moments.body: 17 November 1558: Mary I dies; Elizabeth, aged 25, becomes queen. England is divided, exhausted by religious reversals (Henry's Protestant Catholicism, Edward's Reformed Protestantism, Mary's Catholic restoration). Elizabeth must settle the religion question without precipitating war.
moments.takeaway: Elizabeth inherits a kingdom that has changed official religion four times in 25 years.

moments.title: The Elizabethan Settlement
moments.body: Act of Supremacy (Elizabeth as 'Supreme Governor' — a softer title than 'Supreme Head'). Act of Uniformity (revised Book of Common Prayer, attendance at parish church compulsory). Thirty-Nine Articles (1563, finalised 1571) define Anglican doctrine.

quote.text: I would not open windows into men's souls.
quote.attrib: Elizabeth I, reported by Francis Bacon (commonly cited though disputed)

moments.takeaway: The Settlement was deliberately broad — outward conformity required, inner belief left private. A 'via media' between Catholic and Reformed.

moments.title: Papal Bull Regnans in Excelsis
moments.body: Pius V excommunicates Elizabeth and releases her Catholic subjects from allegiance. The Settlement now had to be defended against external threat. Recusancy fines, Jesuit missions, Catholic plots (Ridolfi 1571, Throckmorton 1583, Babington 1586) and the execution of Mary Queen of Scots (1587) follow.
moments.takeaway: Religious settlement and national security become inseparable. Around 200 Catholic priests and recusants were executed during Elizabeth's reign.

now.title: An enduring compromise
now.body: The Anglican Settlement of 1559 still shapes the Church of England — episcopal governance, vernacular Prayer Book worship, ambiguity on the Eucharist. Modern Anglicanism's spectrum from Anglo-Catholic to evangelical traces back to that deliberate breadth. The 1689 Toleration Act and 1828-29 Catholic emancipation slowly extended religious freedom.
now.open_questions: Was Elizabeth's settlement principled or pragmatic? Patrick Collinson's 'Elizabethan Puritan Movement' (1967) emphasises ongoing pressure from a Puritan wing wanting further reform; Diarmaid MacCulloch sees the queen herself as theologically conservative.

items.reflection: The English religious settlement is one of the most successful exercises in deliberate ambiguity in European history. Forty-five years of relative religious peace under Elizabeth gave it time to settle into national habit.

moments.title: Personal Rule
moments.body: Charles dissolves Parliament in 1629 and rules without it for 11 years. Ship money is extended inland; Archbishop Laud reforms church worship in a more ceremonial direction; Scottish Presbyterians resist the new Prayer Book (1637), leading to the Bishops' Wars (1639-40).
moments.takeaway: Long-term grievances accumulated — financial, religious, constitutional. The Bishops' Wars forced Charles to recall Parliament for funds.

moments.title: Civil War begins
moments.body: Charles raises his standard at Nottingham on 22 August 1642. Edgehill (October) is indecisive. Marston Moor (July 1644) gives Parliament the north; Naseby (June 1645) is decisive. The New Model Army under Fairfax and Cromwell is the first national professional army.

quote.text: I see all the birds are flown.
quote.attrib: Charles I, having failed to arrest the Five Members, 4 January 1642

moments.takeaway: The First Civil War ends in 1646. Charles surrenders to the Scots, who hand him to Parliament.

moments.title: Regicide
moments.who: The Rump Parliament and the High Court of Justice
moments.body: After Pride's Purge (December 1648) removes MPs likely to compromise, Charles is tried for treason. On 30 January 1649 he is beheaded outside the Banqueting House at Whitehall. The monarchy and the House of Lords are abolished. England is declared a Commonwealth.
moments.takeaway: The first European king tried and executed by his own subjects. The Interregnum lasts until 1660.

now.title: Restoration and after
now.body: Charles II returns in 1660. The Glorious Revolution of 1688 settles the constitutional question: kings rule under Parliament. The 17th-century wars produced modern parliamentary government, religious dissent traditions, the standing army debate, and habits of constitutional argument. Christopher Hill, Conrad Russell and John Morrill have produced the major modern readings — from class struggle to high-political accident.
now.open_questions: Were the wars about religion, constitution or class? Marxist readings (Hill) stress class; revisionists (Russell) stress short-term political failure; post-revisionists (Morrill, 'Britain's Wars of Religion') stress religion as the persistent core.

items.reflection: Civil wars rewrite political possibility. By 1660 the English monarchy was restored, but its terms had changed forever — and the failure of James II to absorb that lesson produced 1688.

moments.title: The Invitation
moments.body: Seven English notables — including the Earl of Shrewsbury, the Bishop of London and Henry Sidney — invite William of Orange to invade. The trigger: the birth of a Catholic son to James II (10 June) raises the prospect of a Catholic dynasty.
moments.takeaway: The 'Revolution' was a coordinated invitation, not a spontaneous rising. William had been preparing the invasion for months.

moments.title: Dutch invasion
moments.body: William lands at Brixham, Devon, on 5 November 1688 with around 15,000 Dutch troops. James II's army defects; James flees, throws the Great Seal into the Thames and is captured, then allowed to escape to France. He never returns.
moments.takeaway: A foreign army occupies London. The 'Glorious' label glosses a foreign-backed coup — though one with broad domestic invitation.

moments.title: Bill of Rights
moments.body: January 1689: William and Mary jointly offered the throne. February: Declaration of Right. December: Bill of Rights — no royal suspending of laws, no standing army in peacetime without Parliament's consent, free elections, free speech in Parliament. The Toleration Act allows Protestant dissenters limited worship.

quote.text: All which are utterly and directly contrary to the known laws and statutes and freedom of this realm.
quote.attrib: Bill of Rights, 1689

moments.takeaway: The constitutional shift: royal prerogative bounded by Parliament. The succession excludes Catholics permanently (Act of Settlement 1701).

now.title: Constitutional legacy
now.body: The Bill of Rights remains the foundational document of UK constitutional monarchy. The American Bill of Rights (1791) consciously echoes it. The Williamite War in Ireland (1689-1691) — including the Boyne (1690), 1 July OS / 12 July NS — created the Protestant Ascendancy that shaped Irish politics for three centuries. The Act of Union 1707 was a downstream consequence.
now.open_questions: Revolution or invasion? Steven Pincus's '1688: The First Modern Revolution' (2009) argues for a transformative revolution; Tim Harris's 'Revolution' frames it as part of a wider British Isles upheaval. Jonathan Israel emphasises the Dutch dimension.

items.reflection: Constitutional changes that endure often look modest at the moment. 1689 settled the question 1649 had reopened — sovereignty lies with the king-in-Parliament, not the king alone — and Britain's politics have run on that frame ever since.

moments.title: Watt's separate condenser patent
moments.body: Watt patents the separate condenser, a key efficiency improvement on Newcomen's atmospheric engine. Boulton's Birmingham works partners with Watt from 1775. Rotary motion (1781) allows steam to drive factory machinery, not just pumps.
moments.takeaway: Steam is just one strand. Mechanised cotton spinning (Arkwright's water frame 1769, Crompton's mule 1779) was already transforming textiles.

moments.title: First census
moments.body: Britain's first modern census records around 10.5 million people. London is the largest city in Europe at around 1 million. Manchester's population has roughly tripled since 1750.
moments.takeaway: The state begins to count its population in order to plan and tax — itself an industrial-era innovation.

moments.title: Liverpool and Manchester Railway opens
moments.body: 15 September 1830: the first inter-city passenger railway opens. William Huskisson MP is killed on the day — the first widely reported railway fatality. By 1850, Britain has around 6,000 miles of railway.

quote.text: I have lost some skin, but no breath; and my appetite remains as keen as ever.
quote.attrib: George Stephenson, on early steam locomotive trials

moments.takeaway: Railways collapse time and distance. Communication, markets and time itself are restructured.

now.title: The first industrial economy
now.body: Britain's share of world manufacturing peaked around 1870 at over 30%. The model spread to Belgium, Germany, the US, France and (later) Japan. Pat Hudson, Maxine Berg, Joel Mokyr and Robert Allen have produced competing accounts of why Britain industrialised first — cheap coal, high wages, the patent system, Enlightenment culture, empire markets.
now.open_questions: Was the Industrial Revolution a revolution or evolution? Nick Crafts's growth statistics show slow per-capita growth before 1830. The 'revolution' frame has been challenged but the structural shifts — energy, urbanisation, factory organisation — are real.

items.reflection: The Industrial Revolution is the most consequential event in human history after agriculture. It is also one of the slowest — perhaps a century of cumulative change rather than a moment.

moments.title: Society for the Abolition of the Slave Trade
moments.body: Founded 22 May 1787 in London. Twelve founding members — nine Quakers and three Anglicans, including William Wilberforce, the parliamentary spokesman. Clarkson collects evidence; Sharp pursues legal cases. The image of the slave ship Brookes — packed with bodies — becomes one of history's first mass-circulated political graphics.
moments.takeaway: Abolition was a sustained 20-year campaign, the prototype of modern political activism — petitions, boycotts (sugar), visuals, parliamentary lobbying.

moments.title: Slave Trade Act
moments.body: 25 March 1807: the Atlantic slave trade by British ships is abolished. The Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron is created (1808) to suppress trafficking. The US Congress also bans the trade from 1808 (the earliest the Constitution allowed).
moments.takeaway: Trade abolition was widely supported. Slavery itself within British colonies continued for another generation.

moments.title: Slavery Abolition Act
moments.body: 28 August 1833: the Slavery Abolition Act passes. Around 800,000 enslaved people in the Caribbean, Mauritius and Cape are freed from 1 August 1834 — initially as 'apprentices' until 1838. £20 million compensation goes to slave-owners. Wilberforce dies on 29 July 1833.

quote.text: Thank God I have lived to witness the day in which England is willing to give £20 million for the abolition of slavery.
quote.attrib: William Wilberforce, on hearing the Bill would pass, July 1833

moments.takeaway: The UCL 'Legacies of British Slave-ownership' database (since 2009) records the recipients — and the families and institutions that benefited.

now.title: Long shadows
now.body: The compensation loan was paid off by the UK Treasury only in 2015. Slavery in British India was outlawed in 1843. The US Civil War (1861-65) and Thirteenth Amendment (1865) ended American slavery. Modern slavery — UK Modern Slavery Act 2015 — still affects perhaps 50 million worldwide (Walk Free Foundation estimates).
now.open_questions: Did economic decline of slavery enable abolition, or did moral campaigns succeed against economic interest? Eric Williams's 'Capitalism and Slavery' (1944) argued the former; Seymour Drescher's 'Econocide' (1977) argued slavery was still profitable when abolished.

items.reflection: Abolition is the canonical example of moral political change. The mechanics — sustained organisation, gradual concessions, compensation that flowed the wrong way — complicate the heroic narrative without erasing the achievement.

moments.title: Great Reform Act
moments.body: Passed after constitutional crisis (the Lords' rejections, the 'Days of May', threat of mass peer creation). It abolishes 56 'rotten boroughs', creates 67 new constituencies (Manchester, Birmingham, Leeds), and introduces a £10 householder franchise in boroughs. Electorate rises from about 400,000 to 650,000 men.

quote.text: The Bill, the whole Bill, and nothing but the Bill.
quote.attrib: Whig campaign slogan, 1831-32

moments.takeaway: The most consequential British reform of the 19th century — but a partial one. Chartism (1838-58) followed in protest at the limits.

moments.title: Second Reform Act
moments.body: Disraeli outflanks Gladstone by passing a more radical reform than Liberals expected. Urban working-class male householders enfranchised. The electorate roughly doubles to around 2.5 million.
moments.takeaway: Reform became politically inevitable — the question was who would get credit. Disraeli's 'dishing the Whigs' is a classic of parliamentary tactics.

moments.title: Third Reform Act
moments.body: Extends the 1867 borough franchise to counties — agricultural labourers get the vote. The 1885 Redistribution of Seats Act creates single-member constituencies broadly equal in population. Electorate around 5.5 million — perhaps 60% of adult males.
moments.takeaway: By 1884 most working-class men can vote. Women, the poorest men (lodgers, paupers) and those failing residence rules are still excluded.

now.title: Full democracy delayed
now.body: The Representation of the People Act 1918 enfranchised all men over 21 and women over 30 with property. The Equal Franchise Act 1928 gave women the vote on equal terms. The voting age was lowered to 18 in 1969. Scotland and Wales now allow 16-year-olds to vote in devolved elections. The journey from 1832 to universal adult suffrage took 96 years.
now.open_questions: Why was Britain's path to democracy so gradual compared to revolutionary France or the United States? The answer is usually 'because gradual works' — but Chartists and suffragettes would have disagreed.

items.reflection: Democracy was conceded incrementally over nearly a century, mostly to defuse pressure rather than from principle. The principle came later, applied retrospectively to a series of pragmatic deals.

moments.title: WSPU founded
moments.body: Founded in Manchester on 10 October 1903 with motto 'Deeds not words'. After decades of constitutional campaigning (NUWSS under Millicent Fawcett since 1897) without progress, the WSPU adopts militant tactics — heckling, window-breaking, arson, hunger strikes.

quote.text: Deeds not words.
quote.attrib: WSPU motto, 1903

moments.takeaway: The split between militant (WSPU) and constitutional (NUWSS) campaigners is one of the major debates of suffragette history.

moments.title: Emily Davison at the Derby
moments.body: 4 June 1913: Davison steps in front of the King's horse Anmer at the Epsom Derby and dies of her injuries four days later. Whether she intended martyrdom or to pin a sash on the horse is debated. The funeral procession through London draws thousands.
moments.takeaway: Davison had been arrested nine times. Suffragette tactics provoked harsh response — force-feeding of hunger strikers, the 'Cat and Mouse' Act (1913).

moments.title: WSPU suspends campaign
moments.body: On the outbreak of war the WSPU suspends militant action; Emmeline and Christabel back the war effort. Sylvia Pankhurst breaks from the family over their pro-war and increasingly nationalist line. Women's wartime industrial mobilisation reshapes the political case.
moments.takeaway: The Representation of the People Act 1918 enfranchised women over 30 with property; equal franchise came in 1928.

now.title: A reassessed legacy
now.body: Statues of Emmeline Pankhurst (Westminster, 1930), Millicent Fawcett (Parliament Square, 2018) and others now mark the campaigns. Modern scholarship — June Purvis on Emmeline, Diane Atkinson's 'Rise Up, Women' (2018) — has emphasised the scale and diversity of the movement, including working-class organisers like Hannah Mitchell and Annie Kenney.
now.open_questions: Did militancy help or harm the cause? Constitutional campaigners argued militancy alienated MPs and delayed reform. Recent historians (Purvis, Krista Cowman) argue the WSPU forced the issue into public consciousness.

items.reflection: The suffragettes are an example of a movement whose tactics divided contemporaries and still divide historians. The outcome — votes for women — was the work of many strands; the question of which made the decisive difference remains live.

moments.title: Wilson's Fourteen Points
moments.body: 8 January 1918: Wilson addresses Congress with 14 principles for postwar settlement — open diplomacy, freedom of the seas, self-determination, a League of Nations. The Points become the basis on which Germany seeks armistice in October 1918.
moments.takeaway: Wilson's principles raised expectations he could not deliver against European war aims.

moments.title: Paris Peace Conference
moments.who: Wilson, Clemenceau, Lloyd George, Orlando (Big Four)
moments.body: 32 nations attend. Germany, Russia and the defeated powers are excluded from negotiations. Clemenceau seeks security against Germany; Lloyd George seeks balance; Wilson seeks his Points. The compromise is a treaty harsh enough to embitter Germany but not crippling enough to disable it permanently.

quote.text: This is not peace, it is an armistice for twenty years.
quote.attrib: Ferdinand Foch, on the Treaty of Versailles, 1919

moments.takeaway: Foch's prediction (June 1919) was off by 65 days. WWII began 20 years and 65 days later.

moments.title: Treaty of Versailles signed
moments.body: 28 June 1919, five years to the day after Sarajevo. Germany loses 13% of European territory and all colonies. Reparations are set at 132 billion gold marks (later reduced). Article 231 — the 'War Guilt Clause' — assigns responsibility to Germany. The German army is capped at 100,000. Wilson's League of Nations is included.
moments.takeaway: The US Senate refused to ratify (1920), keeping America out of the League. Germany was denied membership until 1926.

now.title: From Versailles to the present
now.body: Margaret MacMillan's 'Peacemakers' (2001) rehabilitated the conference as a difficult, partly impossible task — not the villainy that Keynes alleged. The borders of central and eastern Europe, the Middle East mandates (Sykes-Picot 1916, San Remo 1920) and the seeds of postcolonial conflict all flow from 1919. The League's failure shaped the design of the UN (1945).
now.open_questions: How much did Versailles cause WWII? The traditional 'unjust peace' line (Keynes, A. J. P. Taylor) is now balanced by views (Niall Ferguson, Margaret MacMillan) that Hitler's revisionism would have surfaced under any peace.

items.reflection: Treaties shape the world, but they're not the only things shaping it. Versailles set conditions; humans then made choices within them. Both matter for understanding 1939.

moments.title: Hyperinflation and the Ruhr
moments.body: January 1923: France and Belgium occupy the Ruhr after Germany defaults on reparations. The government supports passive resistance by printing money. By November the exchange rate is 4.2 trillion marks to the US dollar. A loaf of bread costs 200 billion marks.

quote.text: Inflation is to the State what drugs are to the addict.
quote.attrib: Jens Otto Krag, later Danish PM, on the German hyperinflation experience

moments.takeaway: Middle-class savings were wiped out. The psychological scar — and distrust of the Weimar Republic — outlasted the immediate crisis.

moments.title: Stresemann and the 'golden years'
moments.body: Dawes Plan (1924) restructures reparations with US loans. Locarno Treaties (1925) settle western European borders. Germany joins the League of Nations (1926). Cultural flowering — Bauhaus, expressionist cinema, Berlin nightlife — coincides with economic recovery built on foreign loans.
moments.takeaway: Stresemann won the Nobel Peace Prize (1926) with Briand. He died on 3 October 1929, three weeks before the Wall Street Crash.

moments.title: Collapse
moments.body: US loans dry up after October 1929. Unemployment passes 6 million by 1932. Bruning's deflationary policies worsen the slump. Nazi vote: 2.6% (1928), 18.3% (1930), 37.3% (July 1932), 33.1% (November 1932). 30 January 1933: Hitler appointed Chancellor.
moments.takeaway: Weimar's collapse was political (the centre parties failed) as well as economic. Article 48 emergency powers had been used 250+ times before Hitler used them.

now.title: Weimar as warning
now.body: The Weimar Republic — a constitutional democracy founded in 1919 — is one of the most studied cases of democratic collapse. Comparative work (Levitsky and Ziblatt's 'How Democracies Die', 2018) draws lessons. Richard Evans's three-volume 'Third Reich' history (2003-08) treats Weimar's failure as essential context.
now.open_questions: Could Weimar have been saved? Counterfactuals: Stresemann surviving, Bruning not pursuing deflation, the SPD-KPD split healed. Each plausible — none certain.

items.reflection: Democracies don't usually fall to coups. They erode through political failure, economic shock and the choices of elites. Weimar's 14 years are a case study in all three.

moments.title: Brown v Board of Education
moments.body: 17 May 1954: unanimous ruling that 'separate educational facilities are inherently unequal', overturning Plessy v Ferguson (1896). Thurgood Marshall argued for the NAACP. Brown II (1955) ordered desegregation 'with all deliberate speed' — the ambiguity licensing massive resistance.

quote.text: Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.
quote.attrib: Chief Justice Earl Warren, Brown v Board of Education, 1954

moments.takeaway: A landmark legal victory whose practical implementation took two decades and federal force.

moments.title: Montgomery Bus Boycott
moments.who: Rosa Parks, Martin Luther King Jr., Jo Ann Robinson
moments.body: 1 December 1955: Rosa Parks arrested. The Women's Political Council (Robinson) had been planning a boycott; it begins 5 December. King, 26, leads the Montgomery Improvement Association. The boycott lasts 381 days until Browder v Gayle (December 1956) integrates the buses.
moments.takeaway: Sustained mass action — most participants were black domestic workers walking to white households' homes daily — proves the model for the wider movement.

moments.title: March on Washington
moments.who: A. Philip Randolph, Bayard Rustin, organising committees
moments.body: 28 August 1963: around 250,000 march on Washington for jobs and freedom. King delivers 'I have a dream'. The march pressures the Kennedy administration on civil rights legislation. The Civil Rights Act passes in July 1964; the Voting Rights Act in August 1965.
moments.takeaway: Randolph and Rustin had organised similar marches since the 1940s. The 1963 success was decades of groundwork brought to fruition.

now.title: Movement and counter-movement
now.body: The Civil Rights Act and Voting Rights Act remade American law. School segregation rates fell sharply through the 1970s; many measures show resegregation since the 1980s (UCLA Civil Rights Project, Gary Orfield). Mass incarceration, voter ID debates, the Shelby County v Holder ruling (2013) gutting key VRA provisions, and Black Lives Matter (from 2013) extend the unresolved questions.
now.open_questions: When did the civil rights movement begin and end? The 'long civil rights movement' frame (Jacquelyn Hall, 2005) traces continuous activism from the 1930s and refuses a clean 1968 endpoint.

items.reflection: Civil rights gains were the product of decades of organisation by named and unnamed activists. The iconic events (Brown, Montgomery, Washington, Selma) are the visible tips of much deeper organising work.

moments.title: Empire Windrush arrives
moments.body: 22 June 1948: HMT Empire Windrush docks at Tilbury. Around 492 paying passengers from Jamaica, plus servicemen and others. Most are former RAF personnel or workers responding to advertisements for labour shortages. The British Nationality Act 1948 (royal assent 30 July) confirmed Commonwealth citizens' status as British subjects.
moments.takeaway: Windrush is symbolic, not unique — Caribbean migration had begun earlier and continued in larger numbers through the 1950s and 1960s.

moments.title: Notting Hill riots
moments.who: White Teddy Boy attackers and Caribbean residents
moments.body: August-September 1958: white youths attack Caribbean households in Notting Hill. Five days of disorder. Kelso Cochrane is murdered in May 1959. The Notting Hill Carnival emerges in response — first as an indoor event organised by Claudia Jones (1959), then on the streets (1966).
moments.takeaway: The post-war migrant experience included both welcome (NHS recruitment, London Transport recruitment in Barbados from 1956) and racist violence.

moments.title: Immigration restriction
moments.body: Commonwealth Immigrants Act 1962 introduces controls on entry. 1968 Act extends controls to East African Asians fleeing Kenya. Immigration Act 1971 removes automatic right of abode for most Commonwealth citizens. The Race Relations Acts (1965, 1968, 1976) build parallel legal protection against discrimination.
moments.takeaway: Britain's borders tightened decade by decade — even as integration legislation expanded.

now.title: Windrush scandal
now.body: 2018: it emerges that long-resident citizens — many who arrived as children pre-1973 — have been denied healthcare, housing, employment and have been deported, after the Home Office destroyed landing card records in 2010. Apologies, a compensation scheme and the Windrush Lessons Learned Review (Wendy Williams, 2020) followed. Windrush Day is marked on 22 June.
now.open_questions: What does British citizenship mean if it can be administratively unmade? The scandal forced a national conversation about borders, race and the meaning of empire's legacies.

items.reflection: Migration history shows nations remaking themselves through policy and practice. The same country can welcome workers, restrict their successors, and deport their grandchildren — all using legal frameworks built on top of each other.

moments.title: Edward the Confessor dies
moments.body: Edward dies on 5 January 1066 without a clear heir. The Witan elects Harold Godwinson, Earl of Wessex, the next day. William of Normandy claims Edward had promised him the throne; Harald Hardrada of Norway claims it through the older Cnut succession. Three claimants for one crown.
moments.takeaway: 1066 is the year of three kings of England: Edward, Harold and William.

moments.title: Stamford Bridge and Hastings
moments.body: 25 September: Harold defeats Hardrada and Tostig at Stamford Bridge near York. 28 September: William lands at Pevensey. 14 October: Harold marches south and is killed at the Battle of Hastings. William is crowned at Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066.

quote.text: Then King Edward came to Westminster towards midwinter, and there had consecrated that minster which he himself had built.
quote.attrib: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, 1065-66

moments.takeaway: Two battles in three weeks decided the succession. The exhaustion of Stamford Bridge shaped the outcome at Hastings.

moments.title: Domesday Book completed
moments.body: Commissioned at Gloucester at Christmas 1085, the survey records over 13,000 places, every plough, mill, fishpond and noble landholder. It is the most detailed administrative document in medieval Europe.

quote.text: So very narrowly did he have it investigated that there was no single hide nor a yard of land, nor indeed (it is a shame to relate but it seemed no shame to him to do) one ox nor one cow nor one pig which was left out.
quote.attrib: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, E text

moments.takeaway: The Conquest created a centralised, taxed, surveyed state in a way Anglo-Saxon England had only partly been.

now.title: 1066 in the modern imagination
now.body: The Bayeux Tapestry (probably 1070s-80s, embroidered in Canterbury) remains in Normandy. '1066' is still shorthand for a deep cultural break — Norman French in law and administration, English as the speech of the common people. The Tower of London, Westminster Hall and a Norman elite stamped on parish churches across the country.
now.open_questions: Was the Conquest a brutal replacement of an elite, or a gradual layering? David Bates and others have shown the Anglo-Saxon administrative system was largely preserved — it was the landholders, not the institutions, that were replaced.

items.reflection: 1066 is the date every schoolchild knows. Its significance is real — a conquest, a new language layer, a new aristocracy — but its meaning was made by what was kept (the shires, the writs) as much as what was destroyed.

moments.title: Runnymede
moments.body: After military failures in France (loss of Normandy 1204) and heavy taxation, the barons rebelled. At Runnymede on 15 June 1215, John attached his seal to the Articles of the Barons. The fuller Charter of Liberties (Magna Carta) followed within days.

quote.text: No free man shall be seized or imprisoned... except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land.
quote.attrib: Magna Carta, clause 39 (1215)

moments.takeaway: Clauses 39 and 40 are the source of due process traditions. Most of the original 63 clauses are about specific feudal grievances — fish-weirs, forest law, scutage.

moments.title: Annulled by the Pope
moments.body: On 24 August 1215, Pope Innocent III's bull declares Magna Carta 'null and void of all validity forever'. Civil war resumes; the barons invite Prince Louis of France to take the throne.
moments.takeaway: Magna Carta failed in 1215 as a peace treaty. Its reissues (1216, 1217, 1225, 1297) under Henry III and Edward I are what survived.

now.title: Foundational myth and real law
now.body: Three clauses of the 1297 reissue remain on English statute books today, including clause 29 (descended from clause 39). Magna Carta as 'foundation of liberty' is largely the construction of Sir Edward Coke in the 17th century, used against the Stuarts. The US founders cited it constantly. Four original 1215 copies survive — two at the British Library, one each at Lincoln and Salisbury cathedrals.
now.open_questions: How much of Magna Carta is rhetoric versus law? Sir James Holt's 'Magna Carta' (1965, 1992) treats it both as a baronial treaty of its moment and as a document whose later use was not accidental — the framers genuinely tried to bind the crown.

items.reflection: A failed 13th-century peace treaty became, by deliberate later use, the symbolic charter of constitutional government. Both the original failure and the later reinvention are part of its meaning.

moments.title: Plague reaches Caffa and Constantinople
moments.body: Yersinia pestis reaches the Genoese port of Caffa during a Mongol siege. Gabriele de' Mussi later wrote (probably with embellishment) that besiegers catapulted plague corpses into the city. Genoese ships carry the disease to Sicily in October 1347.
moments.takeaway: The plague moved along trade routes. Medieval globalisation existed in 1347 — and its diseases moved at the speed of merchant ships.

moments.title: England and northern Europe
moments.body: Plague reaches Melcombe Regis (Weymouth) around June 1348. London by autumn. Mortality probably 40-60% across England. Whole villages depopulated; church records, manorial rolls and parish lists record the impact.

quote.text: There died at Avignon in three days 1,800 persons.
quote.attrib: Gabriele de' Mussi, Historia de Morbo, c. 1348

moments.takeaway: The plague returned in waves through 1361, 1369, 1375 and beyond — a permanent demographic shadow.

moments.title: Statute of Labourers
moments.body: Labour shortages drove up wages. Parliament tried to peg wages at pre-plague rates. The Statute was widely flouted. Real wages roughly doubled across the late 14th century. Serfdom weakened as labour mobility increased.
moments.takeaway: Economic consequences of mortality reshaped class relations. The 1381 Peasants' Revolt was one downstream consequence.

now.title: Disease as historical force
now.body: Modern genomics (Spyrou et al., 2022) traced Black Death origins to the Tian Shan region around 1338. The plague reshaped European economy, religion, art (the Dance of Death) and the social position of survivors. COVID-19 (2020-2023) revived comparative interest. Plague is still present in the world; the WHO records around 1,000-2,000 cases a year, mostly in Madagascar, the DRC and Peru.
now.open_questions: Was the Black Death decisive for the late medieval shift from feudalism, or just an accelerant? Robert Brenner's debate with M. M. Postan argued exactly this question.

items.reflection: Mortality at this scale resets societies. Wages, religion, art, gender norms, urban-rural balance — all shifted. The plague is one of the strongest cases for treating disease as a historical actor in its own right.

moments.title: First Battle of St Albans
moments.body: 22 May 1455: Richard, Duke of York, defeats Henry VI's forces at St Albans. The Duke of Somerset is killed. Henry VI — periodically incapacitated by mental illness — is captured. The first action of what becomes a 32-year dynastic war.
moments.takeaway: The roots lie earlier: Henry VI's weakness, factional politics, the loss of France in 1453 destabilising the regime.

moments.title: Towton
moments.body: 29 March 1461 (Palm Sunday): Edward IV defeats Lancastrian forces at Towton in Yorkshire. Possibly the bloodiest battle on English soil — contemporary accounts put deaths at 28,000, modern estimates lower but still in the tens of thousands.
moments.takeaway: Edward IV's reign (1461-83) was relatively stable. The wars renewed under his son Edward V and brother Richard III.

moments.title: Bosworth Field
moments.body: 22 August 1485: Henry Tudor defeats Richard III, who is killed in the fighting — the last English king to die in battle. Henry becomes Henry VII. He marries Elizabeth of York in 1486, founding the Tudor dynasty.

quote.text: Treason! Treason! Treason!
quote.attrib: Richard III, allegedly at Bosworth, in the Croyland Chronicle account

moments.takeaway: Richard's remains were lost until rediscovered under a Leicester car park in 2012, identified by DNA and scoliosis evidence.

now.title: Tudor mythmaking
now.body: Polydore Vergil and Thomas More wrote Tudor-era histories blackening Richard III. Shakespeare's 'Richard III' (c. 1593) cemented the image. Modern revisionism (the Richard III Society, founded 1924) has rebalanced — Richard's administrative record was competent; the Princes in the Tower remain genuinely unresolved.
now.open_questions: Did Richard kill the Princes? The case is circumstantial. Henry VII had motive too. Alison Weir, Philippa Langley and David Horspool have argued opposing positions on the same evidence.

items.reflection: Dynastic war is messy: shifting allegiances, no clean ideological line, generations of revenge. The Tudor narrative of unity restored after chaos is itself a piece of political work.

moments.title: Henry's 'Great Matter' begins
moments.who: Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon
moments.body: Henry, having no male heir from Catherine, seeks annulment. Pope Clement VII — a prisoner of Catherine's nephew Charles V after the 1527 Sack of Rome — refuses. Cardinal Wolsey fails to deliver and falls in 1529.
moments.takeaway: The English Reformation begins as a dynastic crisis with a geopolitical lock — the Pope cannot defy the Emperor.

moments.title: The Break with Rome
moments.body: January 1533: Henry secretly marries Anne Boleyn. May 1533: Cranmer annuls the Catherine marriage. 1534: Act of Supremacy declares Henry 'Supreme Head' of the Church of England. Thomas More refuses the Oath of Succession and is executed in 1535.

quote.text: The King's good servant, but God's first.
quote.attrib: Thomas More, scaffold speech, 6 July 1535

moments.takeaway: The Reformation in England is enacted by Parliament under royal direction — a top-down political settlement rather than a popular religious revival.

moments.title: Dissolution of the Monasteries
moments.who: Thomas Cromwell and the Court of Augmentations
moments.body: Smaller houses dissolved 1536; larger ones 1538-41. Around 800 religious houses closed; over 10,000 monks, nuns and friars displaced. The Pilgrimage of Grace (October 1536) — perhaps 40,000 northern rebels — was suppressed by Henry's broken promises.
moments.takeaway: Crown wealth doubled briefly; most land was sold to gentry buyers, creating a class invested in not reversing the Reformation.

now.title: Five centuries of consequence
now.body: The Church of England remains established. The Royal Supremacy survives in form — the monarch is still Supreme Governor. Catholic emancipation came only in 1829. Eamon Duffy, Diarmaid MacCulloch and Alec Ryrie have produced the modern scholarly synthesis: a slow, contested, top-down change with deep popular reluctance.
now.open_questions: Was the English Reformation Henry VIII's personal project that became something else, or a wider movement Henry rode? The balance has shifted with each generation of historians.

items.reflection: Personal motives (a male heir, Anne Boleyn, monastic wealth) and structural pressures (Lutheran Reformation, fiscal need, Pope's captivity) collide in 1533-34. Both readings — accident and inevitability — capture part of the truth.

moments.title: Elizabeth's accession
moments.body: 17 November 1558: Mary I dies; Elizabeth, aged 25, becomes queen. England is divided, exhausted by religious reversals (Henry's Protestant Catholicism, Edward's Reformed Protestantism, Mary's Catholic restoration). Elizabeth must settle the religion question without precipitating war.
moments.takeaway: Elizabeth inherits a kingdom that has changed official religion four times in 25 years.

moments.title: The Elizabethan Settlement
moments.body: Act of Supremacy (Elizabeth as 'Supreme Governor' — a softer title than 'Supreme Head'). Act of Uniformity (revised Book of Common Prayer, attendance at parish church compulsory). Thirty-Nine Articles (1563, finalised 1571) define Anglican doctrine.

quote.text: I would not open windows into men's souls.
quote.attrib: Elizabeth I, reported by Francis Bacon (commonly cited though disputed)

moments.takeaway: The Settlement was deliberately broad — outward conformity required, inner belief left private. A 'via media' between Catholic and Reformed.

moments.title: Papal Bull Regnans in Excelsis
moments.body: Pius V excommunicates Elizabeth and releases her Catholic subjects from allegiance. The Settlement now had to be defended against external threat. Recusancy fines, Jesuit missions, Catholic plots (Ridolfi 1571, Throckmorton 1583, Babington 1586) and the execution of Mary Queen of Scots (1587) follow.
moments.takeaway: Religious settlement and national security become inseparable. Around 200 Catholic priests and recusants were executed during Elizabeth's reign.

now.title: An enduring compromise
now.body: The Anglican Settlement of 1559 still shapes the Church of England — episcopal governance, vernacular Prayer Book worship, ambiguity on the Eucharist. Modern Anglicanism's spectrum from Anglo-Catholic to evangelical traces back to that deliberate breadth. The 1689 Toleration Act and 1828-29 Catholic emancipation slowly extended religious freedom.
now.open_questions: Was Elizabeth's settlement principled or pragmatic? Patrick Collinson's 'Elizabethan Puritan Movement' (1967) emphasises ongoing pressure from a Puritan wing wanting further reform; Diarmaid MacCulloch sees the queen herself as theologically conservative.

items.reflection: The English religious settlement is one of the most successful exercises in deliberate ambiguity in European history. Forty-five years of relative religious peace under Elizabeth gave it time to settle into national habit.

moments.title: Personal Rule
moments.body: Charles dissolves Parliament in 1629 and rules without it for 11 years. Ship money is extended inland; Archbishop Laud reforms church worship in a more ceremonial direction; Scottish Presbyterians resist the new Prayer Book (1637), leading to the Bishops' Wars (1639-40).
moments.takeaway: Long-term grievances accumulated — financial, religious, constitutional. The Bishops' Wars forced Charles to recall Parliament for funds.

moments.title: Civil War begins
moments.body: Charles raises his standard at Nottingham on 22 August 1642. Edgehill (October) is indecisive. Marston Moor (July 1644) gives Parliament the north; Naseby (June 1645) is decisive. The New Model Army under Fairfax and Cromwell is the first national professional army.

quote.text: I see all the birds are flown.
quote.attrib: Charles I, having failed to arrest the Five Members, 4 January 1642

moments.takeaway: The First Civil War ends in 1646. Charles surrenders to the Scots, who hand him to Parliament.

moments.title: Regicide
moments.who: The Rump Parliament and the High Court of Justice
moments.body: After Pride's Purge (December 1648) removes MPs likely to compromise, Charles is tried for treason. On 30 January 1649 he is beheaded outside the Banqueting House at Whitehall. The monarchy and the House of Lords are abolished. England is declared a Commonwealth.
moments.takeaway: The first European king tried and executed by his own subjects. The Interregnum lasts until 1660.

now.title: Restoration and after
now.body: Charles II returns in 1660. The Glorious Revolution of 1688 settles the constitutional question: kings rule under Parliament. The 17th-century wars produced modern parliamentary government, religious dissent traditions, the standing army debate, and habits of constitutional argument. Christopher Hill, Conrad Russell and John Morrill have produced the major modern readings — from class struggle to high-political accident.
now.open_questions: Were the wars about religion, constitution or class? Marxist readings (Hill) stress class; revisionists (Russell) stress short-term political failure; post-revisionists (Morrill, 'Britain's Wars of Religion') stress religion as the persistent core.

items.reflection: Civil wars rewrite political possibility. By 1660 the English monarchy was restored, but its terms had changed forever — and the failure of James II to absorb that lesson produced 1688.

moments.title: The Invitation
moments.body: Seven English notables — including the Earl of Shrewsbury, the Bishop of London and Henry Sidney — invite William of Orange to invade. The trigger: the birth of a Catholic son to James II (10 June) raises the prospect of a Catholic dynasty.
moments.takeaway: The 'Revolution' was a coordinated invitation, not a spontaneous rising. William had been preparing the invasion for months.

moments.title: Dutch invasion
moments.body: William lands at Brixham, Devon, on 5 November 1688 with around 15,000 Dutch troops. James II's army defects; James flees, throws the Great Seal into the Thames and is captured, then allowed to escape to France. He never returns.
moments.takeaway: A foreign army occupies London. The 'Glorious' label glosses a foreign-backed coup — though one with broad domestic invitation.

moments.title: Bill of Rights
moments.body: January 1689: William and Mary jointly offered the throne. February: Declaration of Right. December: Bill of Rights — no royal suspending of laws, no standing army in peacetime without Parliament's consent, free elections, free speech in Parliament. The Toleration Act allows Protestant dissenters limited worship.

quote.text: All which are utterly and directly contrary to the known laws and statutes and freedom of this realm.
quote.attrib: Bill of Rights, 1689

moments.takeaway: The constitutional shift: royal prerogative bounded by Parliament. The succession excludes Catholics permanently (Act of Settlement 1701).

now.title: Constitutional legacy
now.body: The Bill of Rights remains the foundational document of UK constitutional monarchy. The American Bill of Rights (1791) consciously echoes it. The Williamite War in Ireland (1689-1691) — including the Boyne (1690), 1 July OS / 12 July NS — created the Protestant Ascendancy that shaped Irish politics for three centuries. The Act of Union 1707 was a downstream consequence.
now.open_questions: Revolution or invasion? Steven Pincus's '1688: The First Modern Revolution' (2009) argues for a transformative revolution; Tim Harris's 'Revolution' frames it as part of a wider British Isles upheaval. Jonathan Israel emphasises the Dutch dimension.

items.reflection: Constitutional changes that endure often look modest at the moment. 1689 settled the question 1649 had reopened — sovereignty lies with the king-in-Parliament, not the king alone — and Britain's politics have run on that frame ever since.

moments.title: Watt's separate condenser patent
moments.body: Watt patents the separate condenser, a key efficiency improvement on Newcomen's atmospheric engine. Boulton's Birmingham works partners with Watt from 1775. Rotary motion (1781) allows steam to drive factory machinery, not just pumps.
moments.takeaway: Steam is just one strand. Mechanised cotton spinning (Arkwright's water frame 1769, Crompton's mule 1779) was already transforming textiles.

moments.title: First census
moments.body: Britain's first modern census records around 10.5 million people. London is the largest city in Europe at around 1 million. Manchester's population has roughly tripled since 1750.
moments.takeaway: The state begins to count its population in order to plan and tax — itself an industrial-era innovation.

moments.title: Liverpool and Manchester Railway opens
moments.body: 15 September 1830: the first inter-city passenger railway opens. William Huskisson MP is killed on the day — the first widely reported railway fatality. By 1850, Britain has around 6,000 miles of railway.

quote.text: I have lost some skin, but no breath; and my appetite remains as keen as ever.
quote.attrib: George Stephenson, on early steam locomotive trials

moments.takeaway: Railways collapse time and distance. Communication, markets and time itself are restructured.

now.title: The first industrial economy
now.body: Britain's share of world manufacturing peaked around 1870 at over 30%. The model spread to Belgium, Germany, the US, France and (later) Japan. Pat Hudson, Maxine Berg, Joel Mokyr and Robert Allen have produced competing accounts of why Britain industrialised first — cheap coal, high wages, the patent system, Enlightenment culture, empire markets.
now.open_questions: Was the Industrial Revolution a revolution or evolution? Nick Crafts's growth statistics show slow per-capita growth before 1830. The 'revolution' frame has been challenged but the structural shifts — energy, urbanisation, factory organisation — are real.

items.reflection: The Industrial Revolution is the most consequential event in human history after agriculture. It is also one of the slowest — perhaps a century of cumulative change rather than a moment.

moments.title: Society for the Abolition of the Slave Trade
moments.body: Founded 22 May 1787 in London. Twelve founding members — nine Quakers and three Anglicans, including William Wilberforce, the parliamentary spokesman. Clarkson collects evidence; Sharp pursues legal cases. The image of the slave ship Brookes — packed with bodies — becomes one of history's first mass-circulated political graphics.
moments.takeaway: Abolition was a sustained 20-year campaign, the prototype of modern political activism — petitions, boycotts (sugar), visuals, parliamentary lobbying.

moments.title: Slave Trade Act
moments.body: 25 March 1807: the Atlantic slave trade by British ships is abolished. The Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron is created (1808) to suppress trafficking. The US Congress also bans the trade from 1808 (the earliest the Constitution allowed).
moments.takeaway: Trade abolition was widely supported. Slavery itself within British colonies continued for another generation.

moments.title: Slavery Abolition Act
moments.body: 28 August 1833: the Slavery Abolition Act passes. Around 800,000 enslaved people in the Caribbean, Mauritius and Cape are freed from 1 August 1834 — initially as 'apprentices' until 1838. £20 million compensation goes to slave-owners. Wilberforce dies on 29 July 1833.

quote.text: Thank God I have lived to witness the day in which England is willing to give £20 million for the abolition of slavery.
quote.attrib: William Wilberforce, on hearing the Bill would pass, July 1833

moments.takeaway: The UCL 'Legacies of British Slave-ownership' database (since 2009) records the recipients — and the families and institutions that benefited.

now.title: Long shadows
now.body: The compensation loan was paid off by the UK Treasury only in 2015. Slavery in British India was outlawed in 1843. The US Civil War (1861-65) and Thirteenth Amendment (1865) ended American slavery. Modern slavery — UK Modern Slavery Act 2015 — still affects perhaps 50 million worldwide (Walk Free Foundation estimates).
now.open_questions: Did economic decline of slavery enable abolition, or did moral campaigns succeed against economic interest? Eric Williams's 'Capitalism and Slavery' (1944) argued the former; Seymour Drescher's 'Econocide' (1977) argued slavery was still profitable when abolished.

items.reflection: Abolition is the canonical example of moral political change. The mechanics — sustained organisation, gradual concessions, compensation that flowed the wrong way — complicate the heroic narrative without erasing the achievement.

moments.title: Great Reform Act
moments.body: Passed after constitutional crisis (the Lords' rejections, the 'Days of May', threat of mass peer creation). It abolishes 56 'rotten boroughs', creates 67 new constituencies (Manchester, Birmingham, Leeds), and introduces a £10 householder franchise in boroughs. Electorate rises from about 400,000 to 650,000 men.

quote.text: The Bill, the whole Bill, and nothing but the Bill.
quote.attrib: Whig campaign slogan, 1831-32

moments.takeaway: The most consequential British reform of the 19th century — but a partial one. Chartism (1838-58) followed in protest at the limits.

moments.title: Second Reform Act
moments.body: Disraeli outflanks Gladstone by passing a more radical reform than Liberals expected. Urban working-class male householders enfranchised. The electorate roughly doubles to around 2.5 million.
moments.takeaway: Reform became politically inevitable — the question was who would get credit. Disraeli's 'dishing the Whigs' is a classic of parliamentary tactics.

moments.title: Third Reform Act
moments.body: Extends the 1867 borough franchise to counties — agricultural labourers get the vote. The 1885 Redistribution of Seats Act creates single-member constituencies broadly equal in population. Electorate around 5.5 million — perhaps 60% of adult males.
moments.takeaway: By 1884 most working-class men can vote. Women, the poorest men (lodgers, paupers) and those failing residence rules are still excluded.

now.title: Full democracy delayed
now.body: The Representation of the People Act 1918 enfranchised all men over 21 and women over 30 with property. The Equal Franchise Act 1928 gave women the vote on equal terms. The voting age was lowered to 18 in 1969. Scotland and Wales now allow 16-year-olds to vote in devolved elections. The journey from 1832 to universal adult suffrage took 96 years.
now.open_questions: Why was Britain's path to democracy so gradual compared to revolutionary France or the United States? The answer is usually 'because gradual works' — but Chartists and suffragettes would have disagreed.

items.reflection: Democracy was conceded incrementally over nearly a century, mostly to defuse pressure rather than from principle. The principle came later, applied retrospectively to a series of pragmatic deals.

moments.title: WSPU founded
moments.body: Founded in Manchester on 10 October 1903 with motto 'Deeds not words'. After decades of constitutional campaigning (NUWSS under Millicent Fawcett since 1897) without progress, the WSPU adopts militant tactics — heckling, window-breaking, arson, hunger strikes.

quote.text: Deeds not words.
quote.attrib: WSPU motto, 1903

moments.takeaway: The split between militant (WSPU) and constitutional (NUWSS) campaigners is one of the major debates of suffragette history.

moments.title: Emily Davison at the Derby
moments.body: 4 June 1913: Davison steps in front of the King's horse Anmer at the Epsom Derby and dies of her injuries four days later. Whether she intended martyrdom or to pin a sash on the horse is debated. The funeral procession through London draws thousands.
moments.takeaway: Davison had been arrested nine times. Suffragette tactics provoked harsh response — force-feeding of hunger strikers, the 'Cat and Mouse' Act (1913).

moments.title: WSPU suspends campaign
moments.body: On the outbreak of war the WSPU suspends militant action; Emmeline and Christabel back the war effort. Sylvia Pankhurst breaks from the family over their pro-war and increasingly nationalist line. Women's wartime industrial mobilisation reshapes the political case.
moments.takeaway: The Representation of the People Act 1918 enfranchised women over 30 with property; equal franchise came in 1928.

now.title: A reassessed legacy
now.body: Statues of Emmeline Pankhurst (Westminster, 1930), Millicent Fawcett (Parliament Square, 2018) and others now mark the campaigns. Modern scholarship — June Purvis on Emmeline, Diane Atkinson's 'Rise Up, Women' (2018) — has emphasised the scale and diversity of the movement, including working-class organisers like Hannah Mitchell and Annie Kenney.
now.open_questions: Did militancy help or harm the cause? Constitutional campaigners argued militancy alienated MPs and delayed reform. Recent historians (Purvis, Krista Cowman) argue the WSPU forced the issue into public consciousness.

items.reflection: The suffragettes are an example of a movement whose tactics divided contemporaries and still divide historians. The outcome — votes for women — was the work of many strands; the question of which made the decisive difference remains live.

moments.title: Wilson's Fourteen Points
moments.body: 8 January 1918: Wilson addresses Congress with 14 principles for postwar settlement — open diplomacy, freedom of the seas, self-determination, a League of Nations. The Points become the basis on which Germany seeks armistice in October 1918.
moments.takeaway: Wilson's principles raised expectations he could not deliver against European war aims.

moments.title: Paris Peace Conference
moments.who: Wilson, Clemenceau, Lloyd George, Orlando (Big Four)
moments.body: 32 nations attend. Germany, Russia and the defeated powers are excluded from negotiations. Clemenceau seeks security against Germany; Lloyd George seeks balance; Wilson seeks his Points. The compromise is a treaty harsh enough to embitter Germany but not crippling enough to disable it permanently.

quote.text: This is not peace, it is an armistice for twenty years.
quote.attrib: Ferdinand Foch, on the Treaty of Versailles, 1919

moments.takeaway: Foch's prediction (June 1919) was off by 65 days. WWII began 20 years and 65 days later.

moments.title: Treaty of Versailles signed
moments.body: 28 June 1919, five years to the day after Sarajevo. Germany loses 13% of European territory and all colonies. Reparations are set at 132 billion gold marks (later reduced). Article 231 — the 'War Guilt Clause' — assigns responsibility to Germany. The German army is capped at 100,000. Wilson's League of Nations is included.
moments.takeaway: The US Senate refused to ratify (1920), keeping America out of the League. Germany was denied membership until 1926.

now.title: From Versailles to the present
now.body: Margaret MacMillan's 'Peacemakers' (2001) rehabilitated the conference as a difficult, partly impossible task — not the villainy that Keynes alleged. The borders of central and eastern Europe, the Middle East mandates (Sykes-Picot 1916, San Remo 1920) and the seeds of postcolonial conflict all flow from 1919. The League's failure shaped the design of the UN (1945).
now.open_questions: How much did Versailles cause WWII? The traditional 'unjust peace' line (Keynes, A. J. P. Taylor) is now balanced by views (Niall Ferguson, Margaret MacMillan) that Hitler's revisionism would have surfaced under any peace.

items.reflection: Treaties shape the world, but they're not the only things shaping it. Versailles set conditions; humans then made choices within them. Both matter for understanding 1939.

moments.title: Truman Doctrine
moments.body: 12 March 1947: Truman addresses Congress to pledge aid to Greece and Turkey to resist communist insurgency. The framing — 'free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation' — extends US commitment beyond the wartime alliance to general containment of Soviet expansion.

quote.text: It must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures.
quote.attrib: Harry Truman, 12 March 1947

moments.takeaway: George Kennan's 'Long Telegram' (February 1946) and 'X-Article' (July 1947) provided the intellectual basis for containment.

moments.title: Marshall Plan announced
moments.body: 5 June 1947: Secretary of State Marshall announces a European Recovery Programme at Harvard. From 1948-1952, around $13 billion (over $150 billion in 2020 dollars) flows to 16 Western European countries. The USSR and Eastern bloc refuse participation.
moments.takeaway: The Plan paired economic generosity with strategic intent — preventing communist victory in war-shattered Western Europe.

moments.title: Berlin Blockade and Airlift
