The 'Concert of Europe' framework has been compared to Yalta-Potsdam (1945) and the UN system. Vienna's combination of legitimacy and great-power consensus produced rare durability.
now.open_questions: Was Vienna a triumph of statesmanship or repression? Both — the absence of major war was bought partly by suppressing liberal revolution. Different scholarly traditions weight the trade-off differently.

items.reflection: Diplomacy can produce long peace, but at the cost of freezing political evolution. Vienna kept Europe quiet for a generation by entrenching conservatism. When the freeze cracked in 1848, it cracked deeply.

moments.title: Estates-General to Bastille
moments.who: Louis XVI, Necker, the Third Estate
moments.body: May 1789: Estates-General meets at Versailles for the first time since 1614. The Third Estate demands voting by head, not by order. Tennis Court Oath (20 June). National Assembly. 14 July: Parisian crowd storms the Bastille after Necker's dismissal. The revolution is in the streets.
moments.takeaway: Fiscal crisis (debt from American war), bread shortages, Enlightenment ideas and a weak king combined.

moments.title: Declaration of the Rights of Man
moments.body: 26 August 1789: Declaration of the Rights of Man and the Citizen. 'Men are born and remain free and equal in rights.' Feudal privileges had been abolished in the Night of 4 August. Church property nationalised (November); Civil Constitution of the Clergy (July 1790).

quote.text: Men are born and remain free and equal in rights.
quote.attrib: Declaration of the Rights of Man, Article 1, 1789

moments.takeaway: The Declaration was translated, copied, and cited globally — from Haiti (1791) to the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

moments.title: Terror
moments.who: Robespierre and the Committee of Public Safety
moments.body: January 1793: Louis XVI executed. War with Britain, Austria, Prussia. Levée en masse (August 1793). The Terror: perhaps 17,000 official executions and many more died in prison or extra-judicially. 28 July 1794: Robespierre himself guillotined.
moments.takeaway: The Revolution invented modern political concepts — left/right (from Assembly seating), citizen, revolutionary calendar — and the modern terror state.

now.title: The revolution that won't end
now.body: Francois Furet argued the French Revolution finally ended around 1880 with the Third Republic. Others (Eric Hobsbawm) extend the revolutionary cycle to 1989. The Revolution shaped modern French identity, secularism (laïcité), and the global vocabulary of political change.
now.open_questions: Was the Terror an aberration or the Revolution's logical conclusion? Francois Furet (revisionist, 1978) argued for ideological continuity from 1789 to 1794; sympathisers see the Terror as wartime emergency.

items.reflection: 1789 made every subsequent political revolution legible. Its language — rights, citizenship, constitution, terror, reaction — frames how we understand political change two centuries later.

moments.title: Fort Sumter
moments.body: 12 April 1861: Confederate batteries fire on Fort Sumter in Charleston harbour. By the end of May, eleven slave states have seceded. Lincoln calls for 75,000 volunteers. Both sides expect a short war.
moments.takeaway: Lincoln's position: secession is illegal; slavery's extension is the issue; preserving the Union is the goal. Emancipation as a war aim came later.

moments.title: Emancipation Proclamation
moments.body: 1 January 1863: the Emancipation Proclamation frees enslaved people in Confederate-controlled territory. It is a war measure under Lincoln's executive authority, not a general abolition. It changes the war from a constitutional struggle into a war of liberation.

quote.text: With malice toward none, with charity for all.
quote.attrib: Lincoln, Second Inaugural Address, 4 March 1865

moments.takeaway: The Thirteenth Amendment (December 1865) abolished slavery throughout the United States. About 4 million enslaved people were freed.

moments.title: Appomattox and assassination
moments.body: 9 April 1865: Lee surrenders to Grant at Appomattox Court House. 14 April: Lincoln is shot at Ford's Theatre; he dies the next morning. Andrew Johnson succeeds. The war had killed around 750,000 — more Americans than all other US wars combined until Vietnam.
moments.takeaway: Reconstruction (1865-1877) attempted to remake the South. White supremacist violence and Northern political fatigue ended it in compromise.

now.title: The war's unresolved questions
now.body: Reconstruction's collapse opened the era of Jim Crow segregation (1880s-1960s). The Civil Rights Movement of the 1950s-60s was the second Reconstruction. The Confederate flag, monuments and 'Lost Cause' narratives have been contested intensely since 2015 (Charleston shooting) and 2020 (George Floyd protests).
now.open_questions: Was the Civil War inevitable? The 1850s compromises (Compromise of 1850, Kansas-Nebraska Act 1854, Dred Scott 1857) had failed in succession. Most modern scholarship (James McPherson, Eric Foner) treats slavery's expansion as the fundamental issue.

items.reflection: The American Civil War ended slavery and reshaped the federal state. Its memory and meaning remain contested. The questions it didn't settle — about race, federal authority, regional identity — continue to shape American politics in the 21st century.

moments.title: First Hundred Days
moments.body: 4 March 1933: FDR inaugurated. Within the first hundred days: Emergency Banking Act, Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC), Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA), Agricultural Adjustment Act (AAA), Federal Emergency Relief Administration, National Industrial Recovery Act (NIRA), Glass-Steagall (separating commercial and investment banking). 15 major laws.
moments.takeaway: Roosevelt's fireside chats — radio broadcasts in plain language — restored confidence. The bank holiday and reopening worked partly because people believed it would.

moments.title: Second New Deal
moments.body: Social Security Act (August 1935): old-age pensions and unemployment insurance. Wagner Act: collective bargaining rights for unions. Works Progress Administration (WPA): 8.5 million people employed through 1943, building roads, schools, parks, post offices.
moments.takeaway: Social Security was the most lasting New Deal program. The American welfare state was built on FDR's foundation.

moments.title: Court-packing and recession
moments.body: February 1937: FDR proposes adding justices to the Supreme Court (the court had struck down NIRA and AAA). The plan fails politically though the court reverses course ('the switch in time that saved nine'). A new recession in 1937-38 raises unemployment again.
moments.takeaway: The New Deal coalition (urban, labour, Black voters since 1936, the Solid South) dominated American politics until 1968.

now.title: The New Deal's legacy
now.body: Social Security, the FDIC, the SEC, the TVA and many infrastructure projects remain. The New Deal coalition broke in the 1960s-80s over civil rights and Vietnam. The 2008 stimulus and 2020 COVID relief drew on the same fiscal toolkit at larger scale. The 'Green New Deal' framing extends the brand.
now.open_questions: Did the New Deal end the Depression? Most economists say no — full recovery awaited WWII spending. The New Deal alleviated suffering, restored confidence, and built institutions.

items.reflection: Roosevelt redefined what the federal government did for ordinary Americans. The political coalition that result lasted 40 years; the policy infrastructure has lasted 90 and counting.

moments.title: Birmingham to Selma
moments.who: Martin Luther King Jr. and SCLC
moments.body: Birmingham campaign (April-May 1963): Bull Connor's dogs and fire hoses on children televised globally. King jailed; writes 'Letter from Birmingham Jail'. Mississippi Freedom Summer (1964). March from Selma to Montgomery (March 1965): Bloody Sunday on Edmund Pettus Bridge (7 March) leads directly to the Voting Rights Act (6 August 1965).

quote.text: I have a dream that one day this nation will rise up and live out the true meaning of its creed.
quote.attrib: Martin Luther King Jr., March on Washington, 28 August 1963

moments.takeaway: King's strategy: provoke televised confrontations that exposed the moral character of segregation to the national audience.

moments.title: Malcolm X breaks from Nation of Islam
moments.body: March 1964: Malcolm X leaves the Nation of Islam after disputes with Elijah Muhammad. Hajj pilgrimage to Mecca (April 1964) shifts his view of race. He founds the Organisation of Afro-American Unity. 21 February 1965: assassinated at the Audubon Ballroom, Harlem.
moments.takeaway: Malcolm X's 'by any means necessary' contrasted with King's nonviolence. Both were murdered. The Autobiography (1965, with Alex Haley) shaped Black political consciousness for generations.

moments.title: King assassinated
moments.body: 4 April 1968: King is shot on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel, Memphis, where he had come to support striking sanitation workers. James Earl Ray pleads guilty (1969). Riots follow in over 100 US cities. The Fair Housing Act passes a week later.
moments.takeaway: King was 39. His Poor People's Campaign (his planned next phase, expanding from civil rights to economic justice) was cut short.

now.title: After the movement
now.body: The Voting Rights Act was weakened by Shelby County v. Holder (2013). Mass incarceration (Michelle Alexander, 'The New Jim Crow', 2010) is read by many as new segregation. Black Lives Matter (since 2013) revived street activism. The MLK federal holiday (since 1986) coexists with continuing debates over reparations and structural racism.
now.open_questions: Did the movement succeed? Legal segregation ended; economic and political inequality persist. Different metrics give different answers.

items.reflection: The Civil Rights Movement remade American law in a decade — and exposed how much of inequality was structural beyond what law alone could fix. The dialogue between King's integrationist nonviolence and Malcolm X's Black nationalism still shapes how Americans think about race and justice.

moments.title: Strike begins
moments.body: 1 March 1984: NCB announces closure of Cortonwood colliery. Scargill calls a strike without a national ballot. By month end most pits are out, though Nottinghamshire largely works through. Battle of Saltley Gate (1972) had given the NUM previous victory; Thatcher has prepared coal stocks for a long struggle.
moments.takeaway: Government strategy was set by the 1978 Ridley Plan: prepare for a strike, build coal stocks, mobilise police, sequester union funds.

moments.title: Battle of Orgreave
moments.who: Striking miners and South Yorkshire Police
moments.body: 18 June 1984: around 5,000-6,000 striking miners confront around 6,000 police at the Orgreave coking plant. Mounted police charges, baton charges, arrests. BBC coverage was later shown to have reversed the order of events. 95 miners charged with riot; all acquitted. No public inquiry has been held.
moments.takeaway: Orgreave became iconic of the strike's defeat — and of distrust between communities and police.

moments.title: Return to work
moments.body: 3 March 1985: NUM votes 98-91 to return without a settlement. Miners march back to work behind their lodge banners and brass bands. Within a decade, around 150 of 170 pits had closed. Coal employment collapsed from 250,000 (1979) to under 10,000 (2000).
moments.takeaway: The strike's defeat broke industrial unionism in Britain. Deindustrialisation accelerated; communities lost their economic basis.

now.title: Communities left behind
now.body: Former mining communities (South Wales, Yorkshire, Durham, Nottinghamshire, Scotland) show persistent economic disadvantage — higher unemployment, lower life expectancy, higher disability rates. The 'red wall' political shifts (2019) drew on this discontent. The South Yorkshire Police miners' strike inquiry has been campaigned for repeatedly without success.
now.open_questions: Was the strike winnable? Without a national ballot, working miners and public opinion went against Scargill. Some on the left argue different tactics could have succeeded; others see defeat as structural.

items.reflection: Industrial strikes can be both the assertion and the breaking of working-class power. The 1984-85 miners' strike was the largest postwar British industrial dispute and its political defeat shaped the next four decades of British political economy.

moments.title: Mao launches the Cultural Revolution
moments.who: Mao Zedong and the May 16 Notification
moments.body: Mao, sidelined after the Great Leap Forward, mobilises students against the party itself. The Sixteen Points (August 1966) call for attack on 'capitalist roaders'. Red Guards form across schools and universities.
moments.takeaway: Mao's target was the party bureaucracy. His instrument was youth violence — directed at teachers, intellectuals, anyone marked as 'bad class'.

moments.title: Red Terror
moments.body: Cultural heritage destroyed: temples smashed, books burned, scholars and artists beaten or killed. The 'Four Olds' (old customs, culture, habits, ideas) targeted. Factional fighting between Red Guard groups escalates. By 1968 Mao deploys the PLA to restore order and 'sends down' urban youth to the countryside (16 million by 1979).
moments.takeaway: Estimates: between 500,000 and 2 million killed; tens of millions persecuted; education stopped for a generation.

moments.title: Gang of Four and verdict
moments.body: October 1976: the Gang of Four (including Mao's widow Jiang Qing) arrested within a month of Mao's death. 1981: the CCP's official verdict declares the Cultural Revolution a 'grave error' caused by Mao but credits him as 70% correct overall. Deng's reforms begin in earnest.
moments.takeaway: The verdict preserved Mao's symbolic role while abandoning his economic and political methods.

now.title: An unspeakable decade
now.body: The Cultural Revolution is still partly taboo in Chinese public discourse. Memoirs (Jung Chang's 'Wild Swans', 1991; Ji Xianlin's 'The Cowshed', 1998) have been important. Frank Dikötter's 'Cultural Revolution' (2016) draws on provincial archives. Xi Jinping's rhetoric has revived Maoist tropes, raising fears among scholars.
now.open_questions: How much was Mao in control? Roderick MacFarquhar's three-volume history argued for high Mao agency throughout. Andrew Walder has emphasised local dynamics and factional improvisation.

items.reflection: A national leader weaponised a country's youth against its own institutions for a decade. The aftermath shaped contemporary China's authoritarianism in opposite directions — a hardening of party discipline and a deep aversion to mass mobilisation.

moments.title: Build-up
moments.body: May 1967: Soviet intelligence (false) warns Egypt of Israeli buildup against Syria. Nasser mobilises in Sinai, demands UN peacekeepers withdraw, closes the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping. Israel sees existential threat.
moments.takeaway: Nasser may not have intended war. Brinkmanship escalated past control.

moments.title: Six-Day War
moments.body: 5 June: pre-emptive Israeli air strike destroys Egyptian air force on the ground. Sinai falls within four days. Jordan enters the war; Israel takes the West Bank including East Jerusalem (7 June). Golan Heights taken from Syria 9-10 June. Ceasefire 10 June.
moments.takeaway: Israel triples its territory. The Six-Day War redrew the Middle East and created the modern Israeli-Palestinian question.

moments.title: Resolution 242
moments.body: 22 November 1967: Resolution 242 calls for 'withdrawal of Israeli armed forces from territories occupied in the recent conflict' (the missing 'the' before 'territories' is contested). 'Land for peace' framework. The Khartoum Conference (September) had declared 'three no's': no peace, no recognition, no negotiation with Israel.
moments.takeaway: Camp David (1978-79) traded Sinai for peace with Egypt. The West Bank and Golan are still occupied.

now.title: Permanent occupation
now.body: Settlement building in the West Bank since 1967 has reached around 500,000 settlers. East Jerusalem was annexed (1980) and the Golan Heights (1981) — neither widely recognised. The Yom Kippur War (October 1973), Camp David (1978), Oslo (1993), Second Intifada (2000-05), Gaza wars (2008-09, 2012, 2014, 2021, 2023-) all trace back to 1967.
now.open_questions: Why was the occupation never ended? Israeli politics, US support, Arab fragmentation and Palestinian leadership failures all play roles. The 'temporary' occupation has lasted longer than the State of Israel had existed when it began.

items.reflection: Six days in 1967 redrew the map of the Middle East and created political problems that have remained unsolved for two generations. Few short wars have produced longer aftermaths.

moments.title: State of Emergency
moments.body: 20 October 1952: Governor Sir Evelyn Baring declares a state of emergency following the murder of Chief Waruhiu. Mass arrests of Kenyan African Union leaders including Jomo Kenyatta. The Land and Freedom Army (called 'Mau Mau' by British) escalates attacks on white settlers and African collaborators.
moments.takeaway: The conflict was concentrated in central Kenya, particularly among the Kikuyu. Land alienation by white settlers was a core grievance.

moments.title: Detention camps and torture
moments.who: British military and the Mau Mau
moments.body: Operation Anvil (1954): around 30,000 Kikuyu detained in Nairobi alone. The 'Pipeline' of detention camps held perhaps 80,000-100,000 at peak. Torture and beatings extensively documented. 11 detainees beaten to death at Hola camp (1959) — a scandal that hastened British withdrawal.
moments.takeaway: Most Mau Mau deaths were of Kikuyu by Kikuyu (the 'home guards' organised by the British). The British official figure was around 11,000 Mau Mau killed; later research (David Anderson, 'Histories of the Hanged', 2005; Caroline Elkins, 'Britain's Gulag', 2005) revised totals upward.

moments.title: Independence
moments.body: 12 December 1963: Kenya becomes independent with Kenyatta as Prime Minister (then President from 1964). The state inherited the colonial security apparatus and many of its assumptions.
moments.takeaway: In 2013, the UK government settled compensation claims by Mau Mau victims for around £20 million — implicit acknowledgement of colonial-era abuses.

now.title: Empire's reckoning
now.body: The Mau Mau case opened British colonial archive history. Caroline Elkins and David Anderson's 2005 books used materials newly available. The 2011 'Hanslope Park' files (over a million documents, secretly held) revealed systematic concealment of colonial-era atrocities across many former colonies. Bruce Berman, John Lonsdale and others have produced the academic synthesis.
now.open_questions: How widespread was British colonial violence? The Hanslope disclosures have led to comparable studies of Aden, Cyprus, Malaya, Northern Ireland. The narrative of 'British exceptionalism' (more humane empire) has been largely abandoned by historians.

items.reflection: Decolonisation was often violent — for both colonised and colonisers. The myth of Britain's peaceful withdrawal from empire has been disassembled by historians using the empire's own archives. Reckoning with that record is still in progress.

moments.title: Military rising
moments.body: 17-18 July 1936: army units rise against the elected Popular Front government. The rising succeeds in the south and parts of the north but fails in major cities. Civil war begins. Germany and Italy quickly back the Nationalists; the USSR backs the Republicans; Britain and France impose non-intervention.
moments.takeaway: Foreign intervention shaped the war's course. The Republic was choked by non-intervention even as Hitler tested the Luftwaffe at Guernica.

moments.title: International Brigades and Guernica
moments.body: Around 35,000 volunteers from 50 countries fight for the Republic in the International Brigades. 26 April 1937: German and Italian aircraft bomb the Basque town of Guernica on market day — perhaps 200-300 killed. Picasso's painting (1937, exhibited at Paris Expo) makes it the iconic image of fascist air war.

quote.text: If we lose this war, you and Hitler will be at it next.
quote.attrib: Anthony Eden, attributed warning to Chamberlain

moments.takeaway: The war was a rehearsal for WWII — and a warning Western governments did not heed.

moments.title: Nationalist victory
moments.body: 28 March 1939: Madrid falls. 1 April: Franco declares victory. Around 500,000 dead in the war; an estimated 200,000 executed by the Franco regime afterward. Spain stays neutral in WWII (though Hitler's interventions delay decisions). Franco dies in 1975; democratic transition follows.
moments.takeaway: Franco's Spain was the longest-lasting fascist-aligned regime in Europe — 36 years.

now.title: Memory politics
now.body: The 'pact of forgetting' of the 1977-78 democratic transition delayed reckoning with Franco-era crimes. The Historical Memory Law (2007) and Democratic Memory Law (2022) have begun systematic excavation of mass graves and recognition of victims. Franco's remains were moved from the Valley of the Fallen in 2019. The Spanish right has resisted these processes.
now.open_questions: Could the Republic have been saved? Hugh Thomas's classic 1961 history said the strategic balance was against it. Paul Preston has been the major modern English-language historian. Foreign non-intervention was probably decisive.

items.reflection: The Spanish Civil War was the laboratory of European fascism and the conscience of the international left. Its memory in Spain remains politically contested in ways most other European countries have moved past.

moments.title: Compromise ends Reconstruction
moments.who: Rutherford B. Hayes and Southern Democrats
moments.body: After the disputed 1876 election, the Compromise of 1877 withdraws federal troops from the South. The Reconstruction governments collapse. Within two decades, Southern states pass 'redemption' constitutions disfranchising African Americans through poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses.
moments.takeaway: The federal retreat enabled Jim Crow. The 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments remained on the books but were largely unenforced for the next 80 years.

moments.title: Plessy v Ferguson
moments.body: 18 May 1896: by 7-1 the Supreme Court upholds Louisiana's railway segregation. Justice Henry Brown's majority opinion: 'separate but equal' does not violate the 14th Amendment. John Marshall Harlan's lone dissent: 'Our constitution is color-blind.'

quote.text: Our constitution is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens.
quote.attrib: Justice John Marshall Harlan, Plessy dissent, 1896

moments.takeaway: Plessy legitimised segregation across public life — schools, transport, housing, employment — for nearly 60 years.

moments.title: Great Migration begins
moments.body: Between 1915 and 1970, around 6 million African Americans migrated from the rural South to Northern and Western cities — Chicago, Detroit, New York, Los Angeles. Jobs, escape from Jim Crow, the pull of the wartime economy.
moments.takeaway: The Great Migration reshaped American cities, culture (Harlem Renaissance, Motown, Chicago blues) and politics (the New Deal coalition's Black urban vote).

now.title: After Brown
now.body: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) overturned Plessy. The Civil Rights Act (1964) and Voting Rights Act (1965) provided enforcement. The Shelby County v. Holder ruling (2013) struck down key VRA pre-clearance provisions, and many states have since introduced restrictive voting laws. Mass incarceration, school resegregation and the persistence of housing discrimination extend the unresolved questions.
now.open_questions: Is 'separate but equal' truly dead? Many institutions in the US remain effectively segregated by neighbourhood, schools and prisons even where law is colour-blind. The framework is contested by colour-blind and structural-racism perspectives.

items.reflection: The legal architecture of American racial inequality was built in a generation after Reconstruction and dismantled (in law) in another generation a century later. The social and economic structures it built have proven more durable.

moments.title: Coup of 18 Brumaire
moments.body: 9-10 November 1799 (18-19 Brumaire Year VIII): Napoleon overthrows the Directory in a coup. The Consulate is established with Napoleon as First Consul. He becomes Consul for Life (1802), then Emperor (1804).
moments.takeaway: Napoleon ended the French Revolution as a political process — and globalised many of its institutional innovations.

moments.title: Code Napoleon
moments.body: 21 March 1804: the Civil Code of France is promulgated. Equality before the law, secular legal framework, property rights, no privilege of birth. Translated and imitated across Europe — Belgium, Netherlands, parts of Germany and Italy adopt versions; Louisiana's law derives from it.
moments.takeaway: The Code is Napoleon's most durable creation. It still forms the basis of French and many other countries' civil law.

moments.title: Russia to St Helena
moments.who: Napoleon and the Sixth and Seventh Coalitions
moments.body: June 1812: Napoleon invades Russia with around 600,000 troops. By December, less than 30,000 fit men return. 1813: Leipzig (Battle of the Nations). 1814: abdication, Elba. 1815: return, Waterloo (18 June), exile to St Helena. He dies there in 1821, probably of stomach cancer.
moments.takeaway: Napoleon's wars killed 5-7 million across two decades. They also spread French revolutionary law and provoked nationalism — both major shapers of 19th-century Europe.

now.title: Napoleon's contested memory
now.body: Andrew Roberts's 'Napoleon the Great' (2014) emphasised his administrative achievements; Adam Zamoyski's biographies have stressed the costs. The Napoleon legend (Stendhal, Hugo, the column in Place Vendôme) remains a French national reference point. Recent French debates have reopened questions about his restoration of slavery (1802) in the French Caribbean.
now.open_questions: Was Napoleon's empire revolutionary or imperialist? Both — he spread the Code Civil and conscripted millions to fight for personal glory. The trade-off is the live question in modern Napoleon scholarship.

items.reflection: One soldier-administrator's career altered European law, institutions and borders. The Napoleonic legacy is everywhere — in highway codes, civil law, the metric system, modern bureaucracy — and the catastrophe of his ambition shaped the 19th-century balance of power.

moments.title: Secret Speech
moments.who: Nikita Khrushchev at the 20th CPSU Congress
moments.body: 25 February 1956: Khrushchev delivers a four-hour secret session denunciation of Stalin's 'cult of personality' and crimes — the 1937-38 purges, deportations of nationalities, military failures of 1941, postwar paranoia. The speech is not published in the USSR until 1989, but circulates widely abroad.
moments.takeaway: De-Stalinisation released both reform energies and pent-up grievances. Gulag releases, rehabilitations and a cultural 'thaw' followed.

moments.title: Poznan and Budapest
moments.body: June 1956: Poznan workers' uprising in Poland. October-November: Hungarian Revolution — Imre Nagy's reformist government, withdrawal from Warsaw Pact announced. 4 November: Soviet tanks invade Budapest. Around 2,500 Hungarians killed; 200,000 flee. Nagy is executed in 1958.
moments.takeaway: Khrushchev's de-Stalinisation had limits. The Brezhnev Doctrine (1968, Czechoslovakia) made the limits explicit.

moments.title: Khrushchev's reforms and fall
moments.body: Virgin Lands campaign, corn-planting drive, partial economic reforms, anti-religion drive. Foreign policy: Berlin Wall (1961), Cuban Missile Crisis (1962). October 1964: removed by Presidium in a 'palace coup'. Brezhnev succeeds. The 'period of stagnation' begins.
moments.takeaway: Khrushchev was the first Soviet leader removed peacefully. His memoirs were smuggled to the West for publication.

now.title: What survived destalinisation
now.body: The Secret Speech opened the gap between Soviet ideology and Soviet history that Gorbachev's glasnost (1985 onwards) eventually widened past repair. Post-Soviet Russia under Putin has partially rehabilitated Stalin as a wartime leader while suppressing some of the worst memories. Memorial — the human rights organisation founded 1989 — was shut down by Russian authorities in 2021.
now.open_questions: Could the Soviet system have reformed without collapse? Khrushchev tried; Gorbachev tried later; both failed in different ways. The institutional design may have made reform suicidal.

items.reflection: Telling the truth about one's own state's crimes is politically explosive. Khrushchev managed only a partial version — and was removed in eight years. The question of how authoritarian systems can ever process their own history is still live.

moments.title: Snow's first paper
moments.body: Snow publishes 'On the Mode of Communication of Cholera' in 1849, arguing cholera is waterborne. The Royal College of Physicians and most medical opinion reject it in favour of miasma (bad air).
moments.takeaway: Snow had administered chloroform to Queen Victoria in childbirth (1853, 1857). His scientific work was harder to popularise than his clinical practice.

moments.title: Broad Street outbreak
moments.who: Soho residents around the Broad Street pump
moments.body: Late August 1854: cholera outbreak in Soho. Within 10 days more than 500 people die in the streets around Broad Street. Snow maps cases, identifies the public pump, persuades the parish to remove the handle (8 September).

quote.text: Within 250 yards of the spot where Cambridge Street joins Broad Street, there were upwards of 500 fatal attacks of cholera in 10 days.
quote.attrib: John Snow, 'On the Mode of Communication of Cholera' (2nd ed., 1855)

moments.takeaway: Snow also identified the Lambeth and Southwark/Vauxhall water companies' areas — same neighbourhoods, different water sources — as a natural experiment, with cholera concentrated among customers of the sewage-contaminated company.

moments.title: East London epidemic vindicates Snow
moments.who: London epidemiologists; William Farr at the General Register Office
moments.body: 1866 cholera outbreak in East London is concentrated in the area supplied by East London Water Company (drawing from the Lee). The pattern confirms Snow's analysis (he had died in 1858). Germ theory (Pasteur, Koch) emerges in the next decade.
moments.takeaway: Snow's analysis took decades to be accepted. Public health policy ran ahead of theoretical justification.

now.title: Modern epidemiology
now.body: Snow is often called the father of modern epidemiology — though Pierre Louis (clinical statistics) and William Farr (vital statistics) have parallel claims. The COVID-19 mapping efforts (Johns Hopkins dashboard) drew on the same logic of spatial visualisation. Cholera still kills tens of thousands annually, mostly in conflict zones.
now.open_questions: Did Snow's case actually persuade contemporaries? Some historians argue the outbreak had already passed its peak when the pump handle was removed. The map was more persuasive in retrospect than at the time.

items.reflection: Mapping deaths around a water pump in 1854 made an argument that medical theory then could not. Snow's combination of statistics, mapping and action is one of the most successful pieces of applied science in history — though the recognition came slowly.

moments.title: Madero rises against Diaz
moments.body: November 1910: Madero, after Diaz rigged the election against him, calls for armed rising. Pancho Villa in the north, Emiliano Zapata in the south. Diaz, 80, resigns and flees to Paris (May 1911). Madero becomes president.
moments.takeaway: Diaz had ruled for 35 years (Porfiriato). His modernisation enriched elites and dispossessed villagers, especially in Morelos.

moments.title: Decena Tragica to Constitution
moments.body: February 1913: General Huerta overthrows and murders Madero. Civil war intensifies. US occupation of Veracruz (1914). Convention of Aguascalientes (1914-15). The 1917 Constitution promulgated under Carranza: land reform, labour rights, secularism, state ownership of subsoil resources.

quote.text: Tierra y Libertad.
quote.attrib: Zapata's movement slogan

moments.takeaway: The 1917 Constitution remained the formal framework of the Mexican state until major amendments after 1980. It influenced later Latin American constitutions.

moments.title: Settled into one-party rule
moments.body: Zapata assassinated 1919; Carranza overthrown 1920; Villa assassinated 1923; Obregon assassinated 1928. Calles founds the party (PNR 1929, PRM 1938, PRI 1946) that would rule Mexico for 71 years. Cardenas (1934-40) nationalised oil (1938) and distributed land at unprecedented scale.
moments.takeaway: Around 1 million Mexicans died in the revolutionary decade. The PRI institutionalised the revolution by absorbing potential challenges.

now.title: Mexico after 2000
now.body: PRI lost the presidency in 2000 (Vicente Fox, PAN). Drug war violence since 2006 has killed perhaps 300,000. AMLO (Lopez Obrador, MORENA, 2018-2024) revived populist nationalism. The Revolution's symbolism remains central to Mexican identity even as PRI hegemony has ended.
now.open_questions: Was the Revolution successful? Land was distributed; labour rights established; oil nationalised. But political authoritarianism (PRI), inequality and rural poverty persisted. The judgement depends on the benchmark.

items.reflection: The Mexican Revolution was the first great social revolution of the 20th century. Its land reform agenda, its constitutional innovations, and its institutionalisation as one-party rule prefigured patterns that would recur across the developing world for decades.
